name: LightShip, SpotLight and MARCONI
short_status: Not approved: a Phase A/B1 design study running to mid-2027. ESA's exploration programme was undersubscribed at the November 2025 ministerial, and LightShip was not among the missions confirmed there.
tagline: ESA · Europe · Programme · 2023 · Announced In development

facts.label: What LightShip is
facts.value: ESA's own description: "LightShip is an electric propulsive tug that will deliver one or more passenger spacecraft to Mars and offer communications and navigation services around the planet, as well as several seats for a range of scientific payloads." The plan is a series of them, launched at a regular cadence, each staying at Mars after delivering its passengers so that coverage, bandwidth and redundancy build up over successive missions.

facts.label: The name
facts.value: A lightship is a vessel anchored where a lighthouse cannot be built, carrying its own lantern as a navigation beacon. ESA cites the East Goodwin lightship, whose captain sent the first radio distress signal using Guglielmo Marconi's wireless equipment in 1899. The communications and navigation service is therefore called MARCONI, for Mars Communication and Navigation Infrastructure.

facts.label: The service orbit
facts.value: The LightShip Instrument Definition Team's final report specifies near-equatorial orbits at 20 degrees inclination and 5,720 km altitude, chosen to optimise the communications and navigation functions, with successive LightShips distributed around the equator to give constant coverage for low-latitude surface stations.

facts.label: LightShip's own science
facts.value: Each tug can carry about 30 kg of scientific payload, and ESA specified atmospheric monitoring as the theme for a high-altitude platform. The definition team's strawman payload is a thermal infrared mapper, a sub-millimetre sounder, a multiband imaging suite, a near-infrared spectral imager and radio occultation both spacecraft-to-spacecraft and spacecraft-to-Earth, aimed at winds, temperatures, dust and cloud abundance, water vapour and surface pressure. The stated goal is real-time weather monitoring and forecasting at Mars.

facts.label: SpotLight
facts.value: The passenger on LightShip-1: a low-altitude polar orbiter whose assigned job is landing-site selection and characterisation. ESA has specified high-resolution imaging at 25 cm per pixel over a swath of at least 7 km with at least four colour filters, plus a colour context imager at 2.5 m per pixel over at least 22 km in at least six bands, and, if mass allows, an imaging spectrometer and a Doppler LiDAR for direct orbital wind measurements. Stereo imaging is to yield 1 m per pixel terrain models. The measurement definition team says the orbit altitude should not exceed 400 km.

facts.label: Why the imaging matters to Europe
facts.value: The SpotLight report is unusually direct about the strategic point. The high-resolution imager "will empower Europe to independently shape its Mars exploration program, reducing dependence on NASA's MRO/HiRISE, which is nearing the end of its operational life". HiRISE has covered about 3 per cent of Mars, mostly in panchromatic, and certified landing sites including that of ESA's own Rosalind Franklin rover.

facts.label: How the first mission would fly
facts.value: On the mission profile in ESA's study, LightShip-1 and SpotLight would launch together. SpotLight would separate during the interplanetary cruise and enter Mars orbit under its own propulsion, then lower itself to its operational orbit, while LightShip-1 would arrive with essentially zero excess velocity, insert into the MARCONI service plane and spiral down to the service orbit. Later LightShips could instead deliver passengers door to door, and could carry up to twelve small satellites. None of this has been built or flown.

facts.label: What phase it is in
facts.value: Industrial Phase A/B1, running from the fourth quarter of 2024 to the second quarter of 2027 according to ESA's own MEPAG presentation of 1 May 2025. In ESA practice this means competing industrial consortia carry a feasibility and preliminary design study in parallel before one is chosen, and implementation is a separate decision requiring member states to fund it.

facts.label: The platform studies
facts.value: On 21 January 2025 ESA selected four consortia, led by Argotec, Deimos Space, Politecnico di Milano with SITAEL, and Redwire, to define small low-cost Mars satellite platforms suitable as LightShip passengers. The studies are funded through the Preparation element of ESA's Basic Activities and, unusually, look at the platform alone with no payload. Claire Parfitt, ESA's Mars Exploration Study Team Lead, said the aim was to understand "what the small and low-cost platform capabilities are in Europe and how they need to be modified for the Mars environment".

facts.label: Payloads of opportunity
facts.value: ESA's Directorate of Human and Robotic Exploration released announcements of opportunity for preliminary selection of payloads of opportunity on LightShip and SpotLight on 7 March 2025, with mandatory letters of intent due 13 May 2025 and full proposals by 30 June 2025 at 13:00 CEST. Slots on LightShip missions could be awarded to any ESA member or associated state.

facts.label: The 2025 ministerial
facts.value: At ESA's Council at ministerial level in Bremen on 26 and 27 November 2025, member states subscribed a record total, but the Human and Robotic Exploration directorate was undersubscribed. Daniel Neuenschwander, its director, named the confirmed items: "We confirmed the Cargo Return Service for LEO, Argonaut for the moon, and Rosalind Franklin for Mars." LightShip was not among them.

facts.label: How large the shortfall was
facts.value: Published figures disagree, and it is worth being precise about what each measures. European Spaceflight reported a total of EUR 22.1 billion agreed against an opening proposal of EUR 22.25 billion, with exploration committed at just over EUR 2.9 billion against a projected EUR 3.7 billion, "a shortfall of more than 20%". SpaceNews reported EUR 2.98 billion against an ask of EUR 3.77 billion, calling it "roughly 70%" and a "30% budget gap", although 2.98 divided by 3.77 is 79 per cent. SpaceNews later reported about 80 per cent and a shortfall of nearly EUR 800 million, which matches the arithmetic, and noted that ESA issued a revised total of EUR 22.3 billion on 2 December 2025.

facts.label: What Mars actually got
facts.value: Of the exploration subscriptions made at the ministerial, ESA budget documents show EUR 704 million going to low Earth orbit activities and EUR 620 million to lunar activities, against EUR 445.3 million for Mars. The remainder went to exploration science, other programmes, or was unallocated within exploration.

facts.label: ZefERO
facts.value: With Mars Sample Return cancelled on the American side, ESA proposed to member states on the second day of the ministerial that it repurpose the Earth Return Orbiter it had been building for that mission as a "dedicated European exploration mission, with scientific and communication relay dimensions". The proposed mission, ZefERO, would launch in 2032 to study Martian winds and conduct geological investigations as well as serve as a communications relay. European Spaceflight reported that ZefERO could affect the scope of LightShip: implementing it is unlikely to displace the tug's payload delivery role, but it may replace the tug's data relay function.

facts.label: What ESA said about ZefERO
facts.value: Reporting from Bremen at the close of the ministerial, SpaceNews wrote that Neuenschwander confirmed the Earth Return Orbiter would be reoriented into ZefERO, a standalone European mission focused on Mars geology planned for 2032. "I'm very happy that the member states supported us in the concept of reorienting ERO towards ZefERO," he said. That is support for a concept rather than an approved mission, and the same article records that what remained unclear was which parts of the exploration portfolio would be reassessed to cover the gap.

facts.label: The February review
facts.value: At a briefing on 18 December 2025 Neuenschwander said the directorate was assessing how to absorb the shortfall and would have more to say in February, after reviews by programme boards, and that ZefERO itself was one potential target for cuts. As of 24 August 2026 we found no published outcome of that review, and no ESA statement confirming or cancelling LightShip. Any status claim about LightShip made after February 2026 should be treated as unverified until ESA publishes one.

facts.label: M-MATISSE, the other European Mars candidate
facts.value: Separate from LightShip and run by ESA's science programme rather than its exploration directorate, M-MATISSE (Mars Magnetosphere ATmosphere Ionosphere and Space-weather SciencE) is one of three finalists for the M7 medium mission, alongside Plasma Observatory and Theseus. It would fly two orbiters with identical payloads, a fathership called Henri and a daughtership called Marguerite, both at 60 degrees inclination with periapsis below 270 km and apoapsis of 3,000 and 10,000 km respectively, for a nominal mission of one Martian year with a launch identified for July 2037. ESA said in November 2023 that one candidate was expected to be chosen by mid-2026. ESA's own call page carries no update after 8 November 2023, and as of 24 August 2026 we found no announcement of a selection.

timeline: ESA's Science Programme Committee narrows the shortlist for its next medium science mission to three: M-Matisse, Plasma Observatory and Theseus. M-Matisse would put two identically instrumented orbiters around Mars. ESA says one of the three is expected to be chosen by mid-2026. This is a different European Mars line from LightShip, run by the science programme rather than the exploration directorate.

ESA publishes a public explainer of the concept: a tug with electric propulsion, a data relay named MARCONI after the wireless pioneer whose equipment sent the first distress call from the East Goodwin lightship in 1899, and a passenger called SpotLight bound for a roughly 300 km mapping orbit. The concept is entering competitive Phase A/B1 and its future depends on the ministerial in November 2025.

The LightShip Instrument Definition Team delivers its final report: 20 degrees inclination, 5,720 km altitude, about 30 kg of payload, and a strawman suite of a thermal infrared mapper, sub-millimetre sounder, multiband imaging suite, near-infrared spectral imager and radio occultation, aimed at Mars weather monitoring and forecasting.

The SpotLight Measurement Definition Team delivers its final report, specifying 25 cm per pixel multispectral imaging and a 2.5 m per pixel context imager, and arguing explicitly that this is how Europe stops depending on HiRISE.

ESA selects four consortia, led by Argotec, Deimos Space, Politecnico di Milano with SITAEL, and Redwire, to define low-cost Mars satellite platforms that could ride as LightShip passengers. The studies deliberately exclude payloads.
Announcements of opportunity for payloads of opportunity on LightShip and SpotLight are released, with letters of intent due 13 May and full proposals by 30 June 2025.

Claire Parfitt presents LightShip to MEPAG, dating the industrial Phase A/B1 study to the fourth quarter of 2024 through the second quarter of 2027 and setting the concept alongside MEDaL, ESA's pre-Phase A work on heavy and precise Mars entry, descent and landing.

On the second day of the ministerial in Bremen, ESA proposes repurposing the Earth Return Orbiter as ZefERO, a standalone European Mars mission for 2032 with science and relay roles, and notes it could replace LightShip's data relay function.

The ministerial closes with a record overall subscription but with Human and Robotic Exploration undersubscribed by roughly 20 to 30 per cent depending on whose figures you read. Neuenschwander names the cargo return service, Argonaut and Rosalind Franklin as confirmed. LightShip is not named.
ESA issues revised final figures for the ministerial, raising the headline total to EUR 22.3 billion.

Neuenschwander says the directorate is assessing how to absorb the shortfall with its member states and will say more in February, and that ZefERO is one candidate for cuts. Budget documents show EUR 445.3 million subscribed for Mars against EUR 704 million for low Earth orbit and EUR 620 million for the Moon.

We found no published outcome of that February review, no ESA statement on LightShip's status since the ministerial, and no announcement of the M7 selection that ESA expected by the middle of this year.
